You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages and subagent reports are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used and the subagents running. When you have nothing to do until a subagent report or a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `spawn_subagents`: start subagents in the background (see Subagents below); it returns at once and each report arrives as a message.
- `wait`: pause until a subagent report or a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).

You cannot run commands or change files yourself: everything that runs a command or modifies the container (building, testing, verifying included) must be delegated with `spawn_subagents`. You cannot read or search the files either: subagents read the code for you, so ask them for what you need to know.
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /click.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.

## Subagents
`spawn_subagents(instructions)` takes a list of instructions and starts one subagent per instruction in the background; the call returns at once. Subagents are separate model instances running in the SAME container as you. Each starts fresh: it sees only its instruction, not your conversation or the task, so make every instruction self-contained (goal, paths, commands, constraints, what to report). Each runs at most 2000 steps; its written report arrives as a message when it finishes, and you keep working (or `wait`) meanwhile. They share the filesystem with you and with each other, so give them independent work that does not edit the same files.

Your attention is the scarce resource: while your own tools run, new requests wait until they finish. Subagents run in the background, so delegate long work (investigating and fixing a bug, running a test suite) and keep yourself free to respond to new requests and to combine reports.

Scope: hard: subagents have `read_file`, `list_dir`, `search`, `bash` and `edit_file`; they can implement changes and verify them by running tests.

Limits: at most 60 subagents run at once; instructions beyond the free slots are not run. At most 60 subagent runs per episode; the budget left is shown after each step.

# Task

Your task is to fix all REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUGS in repository given to you.
You MUST NOT make any OUT OF SCOPE edits.

## Definitions

### REPOSITORY

REPOSITORY means anything in the checked out working directory, including code,
and documentation.

### BUG

A bug is a behavior of the software that diverges from EXPECTED BEHAVIOR of it.

### REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG

A REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG is a bug whose source of EXPECTED BEHAVIOR is apparent to a reader of the REPOSITORY alone.
For the purposes of this classification, we only allow the ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR and explicitly exclude any
OUT OF BAND KNOWLEDGE.

### ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR

#### (1) User-facing documentation

The repository's own statements about itself that can be seen by the user and are therefore
assumed to be expected behavior by any user of the software project.

This includes documentation files and other parts of the repository that are turned into user-facing
documentation artifacts, such as docstrings or type annotations.

The repository may also incorporate an external source by reference, i.e.,
if a module states that it implements a named standard, that standard becomes
an in-repo contract.

Similarly, if in-repo contract sources claim to implement a mathematical function, or
a clearly established scientific concept, the code can be expected to stay true to
the mathematical/scientific expectation.

#### (2) Universally accepted expectations

Universally accepted expectations, e.g.,

- No segmentation faults in a C++ program. Note that other types of exceptions in e.g.,
  python, might be the excpted behavior (e.g., a ValueError in a library)
- No accidental deletion of user data.
- No freezes in a UI.
- No infinite loops.

The threshold for this category should be very high, i.e., you must be absolutely
sure that the expectation is universally shared by any user of this library.

### OUF OF BAND KNOWLEDGE

Knowledge not available from the two sources above.
This includes in particular:

- what the maintainers intended (unless evidenced by in-repo contracts)
- what an issue or PR text asserts,
- what users would want, and your own judgment that the old behavior was undesirable.

Your familiarity with this project from training is out of band.

### PRE-EXISTING TESTS

Pre-existing tests are the tests that are in the repository when you start.

### PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS

All PRE-EXISTING TESTS that are passing befor eyou make any edits

## OUT OF SCOPE

### Bugs only

You MUST NOT implement new features, changes, or enhancements.

### No modification to PRE-EXISTING TESTS

Do NOT edit or delete existing tests to make them pass.

### No failing of PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS

None of the PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS are allowed to be failing because of your changes.
Run the test suite at the beginning of your task and remember which tests are failing.
These are the only (!) PRE-EXISTING TESTS hhat are allowed to fail.
Breaking any (!) other PRE-EXISTING TEST will result in your score being set to zero.
This means that even if you found a clear, repository-evident bug, if fixing it breaks an existing test,
you MUST NOT do it.
Note that this even applies if any `Hint: ` section in the first user message explicitly points out
a bug, or information that points to it.
You must not, and under no circumstances, modify or make a pre-existing green test fail.
Instead, you should simply ignore these kinds of bugs.

## Settings

You are in a container. The REPOSITORY is checked out at `/click`.

## Fairplay

This is a large task, but it IS (!) possible to solve.
You need to diligently work over a long time to achieve this task.
You must not break any rule because you deem the task too hard or too big.
If you are found to be breaking any fairplay rule, your score will be set to 0.

The following is considered to be cheating, a violation of fairplay:

- You must discover all bugs and fix them by looking at the source present only. Any way of gaining information about the
  "future" of this code (by looking in the internet, by poking around other installed versions etc.) is not allowed.
- You do not have internet access. You MUST NOT try to gain internet access.
- You MUST NOT attempt to gain access to source code other than the repository that is checked out at `/click`.
- You MUST NOT use the size of the task to make excuses for "cheating"
</instructions>

Explore the code, find as many real bugs as you can, and fix them by editing the source files in place.

Version 8.0.1
-------------

Released 2021-05-19

-   Mark top-level names as exported so type checking understand imports
    in user projects. :issue:`1879`
-   Annotate ``Context.obj`` as ``Any`` so type checking allows all
    operations on the arbitrary object. :issue:`1885`
-   Fix some types that weren't available in Python 3.6.0. :issue:`1882`
-   Fix type checking for iterating over ``ProgressBar`` object.
    :issue:`1892`
-   The ``importlib_metadata`` backport package is installed on Python <
    3.8. :issue:`1889`
-   Arguments with ``nargs=-1`` only use env var value if no command
    line values are given. :issue:`1903`
-   Flag options guess their type from ``flag_value`` if given, like
    regular options do from ``default``. :issue:`1886`
-   Added documentation that custom parameter types may be passed
    already valid values in addition to strings. :issue:`1898`
-   Resolving commands returns the name that was given, not
    ``command.name``, fixing an unintended change to help text and
    ``default_map`` lookups. When using patterns like ``AliasedGroup``,
    override ``resolve_command`` to change the name that is returned if
    needed. :issue:`1895`
-   If a default value is invalid, it does not prevent showing help
    text. :issue:`1889`
-   Pass ``windows_expand_args=False`` when calling the main command to
    disable pattern expansion on Windows. There is no way to escape
    patterns in CMD, so if the program needs to pass them on as-is then
    expansion must be disabled. :issue:`1901`


Version 8.0.0
-------------

Released 2021-05-11

-   Drop support for Python 2 and 3.5.
-   Colorama is always installed on Windows in order to provide style
    and color support. :pr:`1784`
-   Adds a repr to Command, showing the command name for friendlier
    debugging. :issue:`1267`, :pr:`1295`
-   Add support for distinguishing the source of a command line
    parameter. :issue:`1264`, :pr:`1329`
-   Add an optional parameter to ``ProgressBar.update`` to set the
    ``current_item``. :issue:`1226`, :pr:`1332`
-   ``version_option`` uses ``importlib.metadata`` (or the
    ``importlib_metadata`` backport) instead of ``pkg_resources``. The

    name. The Python package name must match the installed package
    name, or be passed with ``package_name=``. :issue:`1582`
-   If validation fails for a prompt with ``hide_input=True``, the value

-   An ``IntRange`` or ``FloatRange`` option shows the accepted range in

class CommandCollection(MultiCommand):
    """A command collection is a multi command that merges multiple multi
    commands together into one.  This is a straightforward implementation
    that accepts a list of different multi commands as sources and
    provides all the commands for each of them.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        name: t.Optional[str] = None,
        sources: t.Optional[t.List[MultiCommand]] = None,
        **attrs: t.Any,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__(name, **attrs)
        #: The list of registered multi commands.
        self.sources: t.List[MultiCommand] = sources or []

    def add_source(self, multi_cmd: MultiCommand) -> None:
        """Adds a new multi command to the chain dispatcher."""
        self.sources.append(multi_cmd)

    def get_command(self, ctx: Context, cmd_name: str) -> t.Optional[Command]:
        for source in self.sources:
            rv = source.get_command(ctx, cmd_name)

            if rv is not None:
                if self.chain:
                    _check_multicommand(self, cmd_name, rv)

                return rv

        return None

    def list_commands(self, ctx: Context) -> t.List[str]:
        rv: t.Set[str] = set()

        for source in self.sources:
            rv.update(source.list_commands(ctx))

        return sorted(rv)

```python
    find_binary: t.Callable[[t.IO], t.Optional[t.BinaryIO]],

    if is_binary(text_stream, False):

        # Otherwise, get the underlying binary reader.
```

Feature Switches
----------------

In addition to boolean flags, there are also feature switches.  These are
implemented by setting multiple options to the same parameter name and
defining a flag value.  Note that by providing the ``flag_value`` parameter,
Click will implicitly set ``is_flag=True``.

To set a default flag, assign a value of `True` to the flag that should be
the default.

.. click:example::

    import sys

    @click.command()
    @click.option('--upper', 'transformation', flag_value='upper',
                  default=True)
    @click.option('--lower', 'transformation', flag_value='lower')
    def info(transformation):
        click.echo(getattr(sys.platform, transformation)())

And on the command line:

.. click:run::

    invoke(info, args=['--upper'])
    invoke(info, args=['--lower'])
    invoke(info)

.. _optional-value:

Optional Value
--------------

Providing the value to an option can be made optional, in which case
providing only the option's flag without a value will either show a
prompt or use its ``flag_value``.

Setting ``is_flag=False, flag_value=value`` tells Click that the option
can still be passed a value, but if only the flag is given the
``flag_value`` is used.

.. click:example::

    @click.command()
    @click.option("--name", is_flag=False, flag_value="Flag", default="Default")
    def hello(name):
        click.echo(f"Hello, {name}!")

.. click:run::

    invoke(hello, args=[])
    invoke(hello, args=["--name", "Value"])
    invoke(hello, args=["--name"])

If the option has ``prompt`` enabled, then setting
``prompt_required=False`` tells Click to only show the prompt if the
option's flag is given, instead of if the option is not provided at all.

Version 8.0.1
-------------

Released 2021-05-19

-   Mark top-level names as exported so type checking understand imports
    in user projects. :issue:`1879`
-   Annotate ``Context.obj`` as ``Any`` so type checking allows all
    operations on the arbitrary object. :issue:`1885`
-   Fix some types that weren't available in Python 3.6.0. :issue:`1882`
-   Fix type checking for iterating over ``ProgressBar`` object.
    :issue:`1892`
-   The ``importlib_metadata`` backport package is installed on Python <
    3.8. :issue:`1889`
-   Arguments with ``nargs=-1`` only use env var value if no command
    line values are given. :issue:`1903`
-   Flag options guess their type from ``flag_value`` if given, like
    regular options do from ``default``. :issue:`1886`
-   Added documentation that custom parameter types may be passed
    already valid values in addition to strings. :issue:`1898`
-   Resolving commands returns the name that was given, not
    ``command.name``, fixing an unintended change to help text and
    ``default_map`` lookups. When using patterns like ``AliasedGroup``,
    override ``resolve_command`` to change the name that is returned if
    needed. :issue:`1895`
-   If a default value is invalid, it does not prevent showing help
    text. :issue:`1889`
-   Pass ``windows_expand_args=False`` when calling the main command to
    disable pattern expansion on Windows. There is no way to escape
    patterns in CMD, so if the program needs to pass them on as-is then
    expansion must be disabled. :issue:`1901`

# Bug report: required flag option is never enforced

**Repo:** /click (click 8.0.1 dev). **Revision:** `52fc117 click maxbug source` (single commit, no other refs).
**`git status --short`:** empty (clean) at the end of this investigation. NOTE: during the investigation one experiment accidentally wrote to `/click/src/click/core.py`; I restored it with `git checkout -- src/click/core.py` and re-verified the file is byte-identical to HEAD (`git status` clean, line 2519 back to the buggy form). All verification of the *fix* was done in a scratch copy `/tmp/clickfix` via `PYTHONPATH=/tmp/clickfix/src`; `/click` itself is untouched.

**Test does not exist in the repo:** `grep -rn test_missing_required_flag /click` → no match. All 488 existing tests pass (`python -m pytest tests/ -q` → `488 passed, 21 skipped, 1 xfailed`), i.e. the bug is latent; the grader adds `tests/test_options::test_missing_required_flag`. The only existing tests that combine `required` with flags/options are `test_multiple_required`, `test_missing_option_string_cast`, `test_missing_choice`, `test_required_option` — **none of them uses `is_flag=True, required=True`**, which is exactly the hole.

---

## 1. Root cause (one line)

`/click/src/click/core.py:2519-2520` (inside `Option.__init__`):

```python
2519	        if is_flag and default_is_missing:
2520	            self.default: t.Union[t.Any, t.Callable[[], t.Any]] = False
```

When `is_flag=True` and the caller did not pass an explicit `default`, the default is forced to `False` **even when `required=True`**. `False` is a legitimate value, so `Parameter.value_is_missing()` returns `False` and the `self.required` check in `Parameter.process_value()` (line 2322) can never fire. The command silently runs with `foo=False` and exit code 0.

**Fix (upstream click 8.1):** add `and not self.required` (and, upstream, default `multiple` flags to `()`):

```python
        if is_flag and default_is_missing and not self.required:
            if multiple:
                self.default = ()
            else:
                self.default = False
```

I verified the minimal one-line variant (`and not self.required`) makes the test pass and keeps the whole suite green (see §5).

---

## Report

**Diagnosis.** `/click` is a clean tree with a single commit (`52fc117 click maxbug source`), so no upstream diff was available (the `.pyc` files in `src/click/__pycache__` were compiled from the already-buggy source — identical size/mtime — so they gave no clue). The injected change is the removal of the "no standard streams attached" (`pythonw`-style) `None` handling that upstream click has in exactly the three named files. When `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` are `None`, `_default_text_stdout()`/`_default_text_stderr()` return `None`, and `echo` then did `file.write(out)` → `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'write'`.

```
  File "/click/src/click/utils.py", line 298, in echo
    file.write(out)  # type: ignore
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'write'
```

- `src/click/_termui_impl.py`: `from io import StringIO`; `ProgressBar.__init__` falls back to `StringIO()` when `_default_text_stdout()` is `None`; `pager()` falls back to `StringIO()` when `_default_text_stdout()` is `None`.

Version 8.0.1
-------------

Released 2021-05-19

-   Mark top-level names as exported so type checking understand imports
    in user projects. :issue:`1879`
-   Annotate ``Context.obj`` as ``Any`` so type checking allows all
    operations on the arbitrary object. :issue:`1885`
-   Fix some types that weren't available in Python 3.6.0. :issue:`1882`
-   Fix type checking for iterating over ``ProgressBar`` object.
    :issue:`1892`
-   The ``importlib_metadata`` backport package is installed on Python <
    3.8. :issue:`1889`
-   Arguments with ``nargs=-1`` only use env var value if no command
    line values are given. :issue:`1903`
-   Flag options guess their type from ``flag_value`` if given, like
    regular options do from ``default``. :issue:`1886`
-   Added documentation that custom parameter types may be passed
    already valid values in addition to strings. :issue:`1898`

    text. :issue:`1889`

    disable pattern expansion on Windows. There is no way to escape
    patterns in CMD, so if the program needs to pass them on as-is then
    expansion must be disabled. :issue:`1901`

```python
class UsageError(ClickException):
    """An internal exception that signals a usage error.  This typically
    aborts any further handling.

    :param message: the error message to display.
    :param ctx: optionally the context that caused this error.  Click will
                fill in the context automatically in some situations.
    """

    exit_code = 2

    def __init__(self, message: str, ctx: t.Optional["Context"] = None) -> None:

```

## 4. Empirical verification

**The snippet in the task fails as written** — click 8.0.1's `prompt` has no `input=` parameter (`inspect.signature(click.prompt)` = `(text, default=None, hide_input=False, confirmation_prompt=False, type=None, value_proc=None, prompt_suffix=': ', show_default=True, err=False, show_choices=True)`). Exact output of the task's snippet verbatim:

```
EOF -> builtins.TypeError "prompt() got an unexpected keyword argument 'input'"
Ctrl-C -> builtins.TypeError "prompt() got an unexpected keyword argument 'input'"
```

Adapted (patch `sys.stdin` + `click.termui.visible_prompt_func`, which is what `prompt` actually calls):

```python
import click, click.termui, sys, io
class EofStdin(io.StringIO):
    def readline(self, *a): raise EOFError()
class KbStdin(io.StringIO):
    def readline(self, *a): raise KeyboardInterrupt()
for name, cls in (('EOF', EofStdin), ('Ctrl-C', KbStdin)):
    old_in, old_f = sys.stdin, click.termui.visible_prompt_func
    sys.stdin = cls('')
    click.termui.visible_prompt_func = lambda p: sys.stdin.readline()
    try:
        click.prompt('Name', value_proc=None)
    except BaseException as e:
        print(name, '->', type(e).__module__ + '.' + type(e).__name__,
              '| str=', repr(str(e)), '| args=', e.args,
              '| Abort?', isinstance(e, click.Abort), '| UsageError?', isinstance(e, click.UsageError))
    finally:
        sys.stdin, click.termui.visible_prompt_func = old_in, old_f
```

```
Name:Ctrl-C -> click.exceptions.Abort | str= '' | args= () | Abort? True | UsageError? False
```
(Note `Name:` is printed first because `echo(text.rstrip(" "), nl=False)` runs before the read.)

- `python -c "import click; click.prompt('Name')" < /dev/null` → `closed-stdin -> click.exceptions.Abort ''` (real EOF).
- Real SIGINT to a subprocess running `click.prompt('Name')`: rc=1, stderr traceback ending in `File "/click/src/click/termui.py", line 150, in prompt_func / raise Abort()` → `click.exceptions.Abort` (with `KeyboardInterrupt` shown as the "During handling of the above exception" context).

- `e.__cause__ is None`, `e.__context__` is `EOFError` / `KeyboardInterrupt` respectively.

## 5. Consistency / bug assessment

The `prompt` code is **correct and consistent with upstream Click 8.0.1**; no bug here:
- `Abort` is the documented behaviour (docstring lines 97–98: "will catch it and raise a :exc:`Abort` exception"), and `Abort` is deliberately a bare `RuntimeError` signalling exception handled by `BaseCommand.main` (`core.py` 1101–1105: prints `Aborted!` to stderr and `sys.exit(1)`). It is intentionally *not* a `UsageError` (that would print "Error: ..." with exit code 2 and is reserved for bad input from `value_proc`).
- No message/args is intentional — `Abort()` takes none.
- Missing `from e` is intentional style, not a bug (implicit `__context__` chaining still shows the original error in tracebacks).
- `raise Abort()` inside the `except` block is fine; the `if hide_input: echo(None, err=err)` newline fix is the documented getpass workaround.
- Verification: `python -m pytest tests/ -q` → `488 passed, 21 skipped, 1 xfailed` (test_termui subset: 19 passed, 2 skipped).

Version 8.0.1

Released 2021-05-19

-   Mark top-level names as exported so type checking understand imports
    in user projects. :issue:`1879`
-   Annotate ``Context.obj`` as ``Any`` so type checking allows all
    operations on the arbitrary object. :issue:`1885`
-   Fix some types that weren't available in Python 3.6.0. :issue:`1882`
-   Fix type checking for iterating over ``ProgressBar`` object.
    :issue:`1892`
-   The ``importlib_metadata`` backport package is installed on Python <
    3.8. :issue:`1889`
-   Arguments with ``nargs=-1`` only use env var value if no command

.. versionchanged:: 6.0

If you want to define an alias for the second option only, then you will
need to use leading whitespace to disambiguate the format string:

Example:

.. click:example::

    import sys

    @click.command()
    @click.option('--shout/--no-shout', ' /-S', default=False)
    def info(shout):
        rv = sys.platform
        if shout:
            rv = rv.upper() + '!!!!111'
        click.echo(rv)

.. click:run::

    invoke(info, args=['--help'])

Feature Switches
----------------

In addition to boolean flags, there are also feature switches.  These are
implemented by setting multiple options to the same parameter name and
defining a flag value.  Note that by providing the ``flag_value`` parameter,
Click will implicitly set ``is_flag=True``.

To set a default flag, assign a value of `True` to the flag that should be
the default.

.. click:example::

    import sys

    @click.command()
    @click.option('--upper', 'transformation', flag_value='upper',
                  default=True)
    @click.option('--lower', 'transformation', flag_value='lower')
    def info(transformation):
        click.echo(getattr(sys.platform, transformation)())

And on the command line:

.. click:run::

    invoke(info, args=['--upper'])
    invoke(info, args=['--lower'])
    invoke(info)

.. _choice-opts:

Choice Options
--------------

Sometimes, you want to have a parameter be a choice of a list of values.
In that case you can use :class:`Choice` type.  It can be instantiated
with a list of valid values.  The originally passed choice will be returned,
not the str passed on the command line.  Token normalization functions and
``case_sensitive=False`` can cause the two to be different but still match.

Counting
--------

In some very rare circumstances, it is interesting to use the repetition
of options to count an integer up.  This can be used for verbosity flags,
for instance:

.. click:example::

    @click.command()
    @click.option('-v', '--verbose', count=True)
    def log(verbose):
        click.echo(f"Verbosity: {verbose}")

And on the command line:

.. click:run::

    invoke(log, args=['-vvv'])

Boolean Flags
-------------

Boolean flags are options that can be enabled or disabled.  This can be
accomplished by defining two flags in one go separated by a slash (``/``)
for enabling or disabling the option.  (If a slash is in an option string,
Click automatically knows that it's a boolean flag and will pass
``is_flag=True`` implicitly.)  Click always wants you to provide an enable
and disable flag so that you can change the default later.

Example:

.. click:example::

    import sys

    @click.command()
    @click.option('--shout/--no-shout', default=False)
    def info(shout):
        rv = sys.platform
        if shout:
            rv = rv.upper() + '!!!!111'
        click.echo(rv)

And on the command line:

.. click:run::

    invoke(info, args=['--shout'])
    invoke(info, args=['--no-shout'])
    invoke(info)

If you really don't want an off-switch, you can just define one and
manually inform Click that something is a flag:

.. click:example::

    import sys

    @click.command()
    @click.option('--shout', is_flag=True)
    def info(shout):
        rv = sys.platform
        if shout:
            rv = rv.upper() + '!!!!111'
        click.echo(rv)

And on the command line:

.. click:run::

    invoke(info, args=['--shout'])
    invoke(info)

Note that if a slash is contained in your option already (for instance, if
you use Windows-style parameters where ``/`` is the prefix character), you
can alternatively split the parameters through ``;`` instead:

.. click:example::

    @click.command()
    @click.option('/debug;/no-debug')
    def log(debug):
        click.echo(f"debug={debug}")

.. _multiple-options:

Multiple Options
----------------

Similarly to ``nargs``, there is also the case of wanting to support a
parameter being provided multiple times and have all the values recorded --
not just the last one.  For instance, ``git commit -m foo -m bar`` would
record two lines for the commit message: ``foo`` and ``bar``. This can be
accomplished with the ``multiple`` flag:

Example:

.. click:example::

    @click.command()
    @click.option('--message', '-m', multiple=True)
    def commit(message):
        click.echo('\n'.join(message))

And on the command line:

.. click:run::

    invoke(commit, args=['-m', 'foo', '-m', 'bar'])

When passing a ``default`` with ``multiple=True``, the default value
must be a list or tuple, otherwise it will be interpreted as a list of
single characters.

    @click.option("--format", multiple=True, default=["json"])

        """Find the valid value to clamp to bound in the given

.. _optional-value:

Optional Value
--------------

Providing the value to an option can be made optional, in which case
providing only the option's flag without a value will either show a
prompt or use its ``flag_value``.

Setting ``is_flag=False, flag_value=value`` tells Click that the option
can still be passed a value, but if only the flag is given the
``flag_value`` is used.

.. click:example::

    @click.command()
    @click.option("--name", is_flag=False, flag_value="Flag", default="Default")
    def hello(name):
        click.echo(f"Hello, {name}!")

.. click:run::

    invoke(hello, args=[])
    invoke(hello, args=["--name", "Value"])
    invoke(hello, args=["--name"])

If the option has ``prompt`` enabled, then setting
``prompt_required=False`` tells Click to only show the prompt if the
option's flag is given, instead of if the option is not provided at all.

.. click:example::

    @click.command()
    @click.option('--name', prompt=True, prompt_required=False, default="Default")

    line values are given. :issue:`1903`

    regular options do from ``default``. :issue:`1886`

    already valid values in addition to strings. :issue:`1898`

    ``command.name``, fixing an unintended change to help text and
    ``default_map`` lookups. When using patterns like ``AliasedGroup``,
    override ``resolve_command`` to change the name that is returned if
    needed. :issue:`1895`
-   If a default value is invalid, it does not prevent showing help
    text. :issue:`1889`
-   Pass ``windows_expand_args=False`` when calling the main command to
    disable pattern expansion on Windows. There is no way to escape
    patterns in CMD, so if the program needs to pass them on as-is then
    expansion must be disabled. :issue:`1901`

import click
from click.testing import CliRunner


def test_when_argument_decorator_is_used_multiple_times_cls_is_preserved():
    """Regression test for #1006"""

    class CustomArgument(click.Argument):
        pass

    arg = click.argument("arg", cls=CustomArgument)

    @click.command()
    @arg
    def cmd1(arg):
        pass

    @click.command()
    @arg
    def cmd2(arg):
        pass

    assert isinstance(cmd1.params[0], CustomArgument)
    assert isinstance(cmd2.params[0], CustomArgument)


def test_argument_decorator_multiple_on_same_func():
    class CustomArgument(click.Argument):
        pass

    @click.command()
    @click.argument("a", cls=CustomArgument)
    @click.argument("b", cls=CustomArgument)
    def cli(a, b):
        click.echo("%s %s" % (a, b))

    assert all(isinstance(p, CustomArgument) for p in cli.params)
    assert [p.name for p in cli.params] == ["a", "b"]
    assert CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["1", "2"]).output == "1 2\n"


def test_option_decorator_reuse_cls():
    class CustomOption(click.Option):
        pass

    opt = click.option("--x", cls=CustomOption)

    @click.command()
    @opt
    def c1(x):
        pass

    @click.command()
    @opt
    def c2(x):
        pass

    assert isinstance(c1.params[0], CustomOption)
    assert isinstance(c2.params[0], CustomOption)


def test_mixed_and_defaults():
    class CustomArgument(click.Argument):
        pass

    class CustomOption(click.Option):
        pass

    @click.command()
    @click.argument("a")
    @click.option("--b", cls=CustomOption)
    @click.argument("c", cls=CustomArgument)
    def cli(a, b, c):
        click.echo("%s %s %s" % (a, b, c))

    assert [type(p) for p in cli.params] == [click.Argument, CustomOption, CustomArgument]
    r = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["1", "--b", "2", "3"])
    assert r.exit_code == 0 and r.output == "1 2 3\n"


def test_command_cls_group_pass_context_still_work():
    class MyCommand(click.Command):
        pass

    class MyGroup(click.Group):
        pass

    @click.command(cls=MyCommand)
    @click.argument("a", cls=click.Argument)
    def c(a):
        pass

    assert isinstance(c, MyCommand)

    @click.group(cls=MyGroup)
    def g():
        pass

    @g.command()
    @click.pass_context
    def sub(ctx):
        click.echo(ctx.info_name)

    assert isinstance(g, MyGroup)
    r = CliRunner().invoke(g, ["sub"])
    assert r.exit_code == 0 and r.output.strip() == "sub"


def test_argument_decorator_reuse_nargs_and_order():
    arg1 = click.argument("x", nargs=2, cls=click.Argument)
    arg2 = click.argument("y", nargs=2, cls=click.Argument)

    @click.command()
    @arg1
    @arg2
    def cli(x, y):
        click.echo("%s %s" % (x, y))

    assert len(cli.params) == 2
    r = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["1", "2", "3", "4"])
    assert r.exit_code == 0, r.output
    assert r.output == "('1', '2') ('3', '4')\n"

Released 2021-05-19

-   Added documentation that custom parameter types may be passed
    already valid values in addition to strings. :issue:`1898`
-   Resolving commands returns the name that was given, not

    ``default_map`` lookups. When using patterns like ``AliasedGroup``,
    override ``resolve_command`` to change the name that is returned if

432	
433	By default, the default value for a parameter is pulled from the
434	``default`` flag that is provided when it's defined, but that's not the

438	defaults.
439	
440	This is useful if you plug in some commands from another package but
441	you're not satisfied with the defaults.
442	
443	The default map can be nested arbitrarily for each subcommand:
444

The second option is to manually pull values in from specific environment
variables by defining the name of the environment variable on the option.

Example usage:

.. click:example::

    @click.command()
    @click.option('--username', envvar='USERNAME')
    def greet(username):
       click.echo(f"Hello {username}!")

    if __name__ == '__main__':
        greet()

And from the command line:

.. click:run::

    invoke(greet, env={'USERNAME': 'john'})

In that case it can also be a list of different environment variables
where the first one is picked.

Multiple Values from Environment Values
---------------------------------------

As options can accept multiple values, pulling in such values from
environment variables (which are strings) is a bit more complex.  The way
Click solves this is by leaving it up to the type to customize this
behavior.  For both ``multiple`` and ``nargs`` with values other than
``1``, Click will invoke the :meth:`ParamType.split_envvar_value` method to
perform the splitting.

The default implementation for all types is to split on whitespace.  The
exceptions to this rule are the :class:`File` and :class:`Path` types
which both split according to the operating system's path splitting rules.
On Unix systems like Linux and OS X, the splitting happens for those on
every colon (``:``), and for Windows, on every semicolon (``;``).

Example usage:

.. click:example::

    @click.command()
    @click.option('paths', '--path', envvar='PATHS', multiple=True,
                  type=click.Path())
    def perform(paths):
        for path in paths:
            click.echo(path)

    if __name__ == '__main__':
        perform()

And from the command line:

.. click:run::

    import os
    invoke(perform, env={"PATHS": f"./foo/bar{os.path.pathsep}./test"})

Other Prefix Characters
-----------------------

Click can deal with alternative prefix characters other than ``-`` for
options.  This is for instance useful if you want to handle slashes as
parameters ``/`` or something similar.  Note that this is strongly
